verbalization: Doxorubicin is implicated in the treatment of Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) through a series of molecular pathways, as evidenced by its association with specific chromosomal translocations. The drug is linked to AML with T(9;11)(p22;q23), which is a known driver of AML and is also associated with the drug Glasdegib and Idarubicin. These relationships suggest that Doxorubicin may exert its therapeutic effects through mechanisms that are downstream of these translocations. The presence of Inv3(p21;q26.2) or T(3;3)(p21;q26.2) in the AML subset further indicates that Doxorubicin may influence the disease through pathways that are not directly tied to the translocations but may still be mediated by the same molecular mechanisms. The integration of these pathways suggests that Doxorubicin could potentially modulate AML through a broader, less direct mechanism, possibly involving the regulation of gene expression or cellular proliferation. The evidence supports a role for Doxorubicin in AML, but the exact mechanism by which it interacts with the Inv3(p21;q26.2) or T(3;3)(p21;q26.2) translocations remains to be fully elucidated.
